title: When the Group Chat Wakes
premise: Quentin Dunmore, a nonbinary statistician who has spent twenty years quietly proving the town's beloved Founders' Game is mathematically rigged, begins receiving notes from the school's legendary ghost — notes written in ink that shouldn't exist, addressed to them by a name they've never told anyone. The ghost is the erased first statistician of the tradition, and she needs Quentin to expose the rigging before the town's centennial ceremony seals the lie forever. As Quentin falls for the ghost's living descendant, Mara, they must choose between the safety of careful silence and a justice that exists entirely outside the law. In the end, Quentin burns their twenty years of evidence into one impossible public truth, frees the ghost, and claims both the name on those notes and a place in the town they'd only ever watched from the margins.
about_author: Gideon Coldharbour is the pen name of a former small-town school archivist who spent years cataloguing trophies no one remembered winning. They write stories about the people who keep score and the ghosts who keep secrets.

chapters.title: The Margin of Error
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Twenty years of scorekeeping distilled: Quentin runs the numbers on the Founders' Game and confirms, again, that the outcomes are fixed — but says nothing, as always. The emotional beat is the ache of competence without courage, ending with Quentin locking the proof in a drawer they never open.

chapters.title: Ink That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A note appears inside Quentin's locked desk: 'You're right about 1974. — E.' The ink shifts color when looked at directly. Quentin tells themselves it's a prank, but keeps the note against every rule of self-preservation. Beat: fear braided with the first thrill of being seen.

chapters.title: Mara Voss Knows Everyone
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara, the school's new archivist and great-granddaughter of the Game's most famous coach, notices Quentin hovering over the trophy case. Their first real conversation crackles — she's warm where Quentin is guarded. Beat: reluctant attraction to someone who belongs effortlessly.

chapters.title: The Second Note Names Me
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The next note uses 'Quentin' — the name Quentin chose at nineteen and told no one in this town. Terror and vertigo: someone knows. Quentin investigates the archive at night and finds cold spots and a ledger missing its final pages. Beat: the careful life cracking open.

chapters.title: Centennial Countdown
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The town announces the Founders' Game centennial ceremony; Mara is assigned to curate the history exhibit and asks Quentin to fact-check it. Quentin realizes the official story erases the original statistician entirely. Beat: duty pulling them both toward the same buried truth.

chapters.title: Eleanor, 1919
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Following the ghost's clues through microfilm and a hidden dumbwaiter, Quentin identifies her: Eleanor Ashe, the Game's first scorekeeper, who died the night she tried to report the first fix. Her notes grow more urgent. Beat: grief for a stranger who feels like a mirror.

chapters.title: What the Trophies Remember
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara discovers her great-grandfather's coaching ledger contains Eleanor's handwriting after her death — impossible, chilling, and proof the family profited from the silence. Mara hides it from the committee. Beat: love of family colliding with love of truth.

chapters.title: Two People, One Locked Room
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Quentin and Mara catch each other searching the archive after hours and finally compare notes — literally. Trust forms fast and dangerously. The chapter ends with Eleanor manifesting fully before them both. Beat: the relief of no longer being alone in the impossible.

chapters.title: Rules of a Haunting
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Eleanor explains her terms: she can't leave the grounds, can't touch paper except with borrowed ink, and the centennial oath will bind her story permanently if unchallenged. She needs a living voice. Beat: hope arriving with a deadline attached.

chapters.title: The Committee of Good People
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara probes the centennial committee and finds decent people defending an indecent arrangement — including her own mother. The rigging isn't villainy; it's inheritance. Beat: disillusionment with belonging that was always conditional.

chapters.title: Twenty Years in a Drawer
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin finally opens the drawer and shows Eleanor two decades of statistical proof. She weeps — ghosts apparently can. But Quentin admits why they never spoke: fear of losing the only place that ever tolerated them. Beat: shame confronted honestly.

chapters.title: Almost-Kiss in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Working late, Quentin and Mara cross the line between allies and something more — then Quentin pulls back, terrified of being known that completely. Mara leaves hurt. Beat: love against the duty of staying hidden.

chapters.title: Someone Is Erasing the Evidence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The archive is broken into; Eleanor's ledger pages and Quentin's copies vanish. Someone living knows about the haunting. Suspicion falls on the committee's chair, but the trail points somewhere worse. Beat: the stakes turn physical.

chapters.title: The Descendant's Bargain
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara confronts her mother, who confesses the family has protected the fix for four generations — and offers Mara a place in it, publicly, at the ceremony. Mara refuses and is cut off. Beat: choosing justice over inheritance at real cost.

chapters.title: Eleanor's Last Night, Retold
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Through Eleanor's fragmented memory-visions, the true story emerges: she didn't fall; she was silenced by the founders themselves, and the Game was built over her grave of a reputation. Beat: righteous fury replacing fear.

chapters.title: Rigged, Proven, Published
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. With three days left, Quentin rebuilds the destroyed evidence from memory and publishes the full statistical analysis anonymously online. The town erupts; the committee scrambles; the anonymous author becomes a manhunt. Beat: the point of no return.

chapters.title: They Know It's You
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The committee traces the analysis to Quentin via the archive access logs. Mara lies to protect them, burning her last bridge home. Quentin, furious at being protected instead of asked, nearly pushes Mara away. Beat: love tested by protection without consent.

chapters.title: What Ink Remembers
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Eleanor reveals her final secret: the impossible ink is made of everything the town refused to write down, and it will only hold long enough for one public reading. Whoever speaks her name aloud at the ceremony finishes what she started. Beat: the weight of a single chance.

chapters.title: The Centennial Ceremony
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Under the lights, before the whole town, the oath is read — and Quentin walks onto the field, takes the microphone, and speaks Eleanor Ashe's name along with twenty years of receipts. The ink-blazoned ledger materializes in midair before everyone. Beat: terror transfigured into triumph.

chapters.title: Letting Go of Eleanor
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Freed by witness, Eleanor fades — but first she thanks Quentin for finishing the scorekeeping she began, and tells them the name on the notes was always theirs to claim. Beat: mourning and release entwined; the ghost gets her rest.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Audited
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The fallout: investigations, resignations, a town forced to rewrite its founding story. Some forgive; some don't. Mara and Quentin find each other amid the wreckage, choosing each other without conditions this time. Beat: belonging rebuilt on truth instead of silence.

chapters.title: The New Scorekeeper
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, epilogue. One year later, the restored archive bears a new plaque: Head Statistician, Q. Dunmore. Quentin writes the first entry of the honest era in ordinary black ink — and smiles at a faint, familiar shimmer in the margins. Beat: quiet joy; the watch continues, freely kept.
